subject: Job Search CRM & AI Application Tailoring Center
text:
Can plain rules replace an AI score? On 8 real resumes they agreed 6 times out of 8, so I kept both and made each show its evidence.

The scores come from Career Pilot, the job-search platform I built and use every day. I built it because the tools I tried over two years of searching were unfinished or failed. Its weakest part was the match score: one AI number out of 100 that never said which skills matched and which were missing.

So I wrote a rule-based score next to it, also out of 100: 60 points for skills, 20 for the role type, 20 for years of experience. For every skill a posting asks for, it shows where that skill appears in the resume: in a job, in a project, or only in the skills list.

The rule that matters most is a limit. A frontend developer posting that also lists Python, SQL, dbt and AWS shares 4 of its 8 skills with a data engineering resume, enough to score 50. Because the role type doesn't match, the score is held at 40, and the AI score gets the same limit.

Then the test, on 8 resumes I had tailored. The two scores were 16.9 points apart on average and agreed on whether a resume needed another rewrite 5 times out of 8. One fix, counting "Tableau or Power BI" as one requirement instead of two, brought that to 12 points and 6 out of 8. Not enough to drop the AI.

So every posting now shows both scores, each skill with the resume line behind it, and a job of the wrong type can't score above 40 under either one.

If you've had rules and a model scoring the same thing, how did you decide when the rules were good enough to replace it?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: Portfolio assistant fallback
text:
When Gemini fails, the chat assistant on my portfolio still answers, with no AI model at all. It got 92.5% of test questions right.

Without a backup, a failed Gemini call means a recruiter's question gets no answer. So I built one that runs in the browser: every fact on the site (each job, project, skill and certificate) is stored as a short passage, a question is matched to passages by keywords and by meaning, and a small ranking model picks the best one. The answer is that passage with its source, so it can't make anything up.

To test it, I wrote 120 questions a recruiter might ask, including typos and questions it should refuse, like salary, visa status and skills not in my profile. I tuned on 80 and kept 40 aside until the end. The 92.5% is on those 40.

The biggest gain came from teaching it when not to answer. Refusing when the ranking model's confidence is low added 4 points, and fixed refusal topics for pay, work authorization and personal details added 7. Together that is more than the ranking model itself added, 10 points.

Speed was the other problem: the first version took 7.5 s per answer. Shorter inputs and a smaller ranking model brought it to 0.9 s, and its 57 MB of files download only the first time Gemini fails. It still misses some vague questions, like "what has he been working on recently".

So a recruiter who asks about my work gets an answer quoted from my own profile, with its source, even when the AI behind the site is down.

If you've built retrieval over a small set of documents, how do you decide when it should refuse instead of answer?

#MachineLearning #NLP

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
text:
An auditor checking a ledger in order opens 1,108 entries to find 90% of the problems. Sorted by my risk score, they open 43.

The ledger is simulated. I generated the entries and planted 47 problems, listed in a separate table that the detection code never reads, so every result can be checked against the right answers.

Each entry gets three checks. Benford's Law: in many real financial datasets about 30% of amounts start with 1, so amounts that break that pattern score higher. An Isolation Forest, a model that flags amounts and tax ratios unlike the rest. And a tax-rate rule that flags any claim whose rate doesn't match its category. The pipeline runs in Dagster, so each step can be rerun on its own.

Scoring each check on its own changed how I read the results. The plain tax-rate rule found 45 of the 47 problems and flagged nothing wrongly. The model found 18, and the rule had already found all 18.

So the rule's 45 flags go first, and every one is a real problem: that alone gets an auditor to 90% in 43 entries. The model and Benford's Law rank the rest, and the 2 problems the rule missed come up at entries 131 and 137 of 1,200.

On a real ledger I would start the same way: measure the simple rules alone first, then use a model to rank what they leave.

How do you get labels for a real ledger when nobody plants the answers?

#DataEngineering #AnomalyDetection

subject: Member Messages QA System: Semantic Search & NER-Based Question Answering
text:
I chose embeddings-based semantic search for member questions, ruling out fine-tuned LLMs, knowledge graphs, and rule-based matching.

To answer natural-language questions about member data, I built an interactive /ask API that ranks unstructured messages by cosine similarity over SentenceTransformer embeddings, combined with spaCy named entity recognition and fuzzy first-name matching.

Retrieving unstructured text can easily pull a message that matches the subject but contains the wrong event details, so the system needed to prove how accurate it was at finding the correct member, message, and answer for a given question.

So I ran eval_qa.py to score 26 hand-written, paraphrased questions against a labelled evaluation set.

The answer was that member identification accuracy reached 100%, while message retrieval accuracy and answer extraction accuracy both reached 96%. The one miss asks for Lorenzo's Thursday booking, where the top-ranked message is his Saturday dinner at The Fat Duck. That result led to a clear threshold: CI fails if answer accuracy drops below 90%.

This system now answers natural-language questions about members directly from unstructured message text.

When your semantic search retriever pulls a message for the wrong day of the week, do you fix that in pre-filtering or during answer extraction?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: Multi-State Land Use Emissions Analysis
text:
Forecasting emissions by copying last year beats two standard models on real state data.

When forests burn or farmland turns into suburbs, a state stores or releases a different amount of carbon. I wanted to learn how that is measured from public records, so Multi-State Land Use Emissions Analysis processes daily land-cover data for five U.S. states. The daily files are simulated, but the emission factors and historical inventory come from the EPA.

Change like this is often slow, so predicting next year as a copy of this one is a strong competitor. To see if learning from history helps more than repetition, I compared Linear Regression and Random Forest against that naive baseline.

The test used the EPA's 25 annual series. I trained on data up to 2017 and scored predictions for 2018 through 2022. Linear Regression reached an accuracy of 0.9418 and Random Forest 0.9329. Copying the previous value reached 0.947.

Neither one beat it, so the report now shows the copy-last-year number next to every score.

If you forecast a slow-moving series, do you report a copy-last-year baseline next to every model score?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: Job Market Lakehouse
text:
A June 2025 query on my job market lakehouse read 3,015 of its 60,000 rows. Hive never opened the other 19 months.

I built the lakehouse to learn how a whole data system fits together, from raw files to checked output. With AI changing how work gets done, I think an engineer has to stay broad and keep adapting.

The pipeline runs on simulated job postings from 400 companies. PySpark transforms them, 11 Great Expectations checks gate the output, Airflow runs the steps, and a HiveQL table keeps the raw postings in Parquet, split by month.

Splitting a table that way only saves work if the engine skips the folders a filter rules out, so I tested it. I wrote one month's files straight to storage, registered them with MSCK REPAIR TABLE as the 21st partition, then filtered on June 2025 and read the query plan. The plan pruned to a single partition, and the query returned only June's postings.

So the split pays off where it counts: a one-month question costs 3,015 rows of reading instead of all 60,000, and the plan itself shows it.

If you split a table by month, how do you confirm the engine actually skips the other partitions?

#DataEngineering #HiveQL

subject: AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits
text:
A drift alert is only worth something if you act on it. Acting on mine ended the run at 83% accuracy instead of 66%.

AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits is a portfolio project that watches a deployed classifier's inputs and decisions every day: drift tests on the features, bias checks by gender and age group, and a table of flagged problems a reviewer reads instead of every metric. I built it to learn how the whole monitoring system fits together, not just one piece, because with AI changing how work gets done, an engineer has to keep adapting.

It runs on simulated data: 60 days of predictions, with drift injected partway through. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test raised the first alert on day 40, without waiting for any outcome labels. That left a decision to make: keep the deployed model, or retrain it.

So I replayed the rest of the run both ways. The catch is that outcomes arrive late, so the retrained version could only learn from the most recent week of labels, each one 7 days old.

Left alone, the model slid from 99.88% accuracy to 66%. Retrained every day on those delayed labels, it finished at 83%, and its total accuracy shortfall over the period was 32.6% smaller.

The alert now triggers that daily retrain, so recovery starts the day the data shifts, not when someone notices accuracy falling.

If you monitor a model whose labels arrive late, do you retrain on a fixed schedule or only when a drift alert fires?

#MachineLearning #DataEngineering

subject: Sales Analytics & RFM Customer Segmentation Pipeline
text:
Three of four customer clusters differed mainly in recency, while only one stood far apart on frequency and spend.

Sales Analytics & RFM Customer Segmentation Pipeline is a personal portfolio project that models transaction data in a star-schema database for business intelligence reporting. Total sales tell how much a business sells, but not who buys. I built this project to learn how to find real customer groups in transaction data instead of guessing them.

Before sending segment labels downstream to reports, I needed to check if recency, frequency, and monetary value features actually split accounts into clear categories.

So I clustered scaled RFM features for 2,000 synthetic accounts using K-Means with four groups. The four clusters explained 93.9% of the variance in the scaled features, while a two-dimensional PCA view kept 99.6% of that variance. One group of 400 VIP Champions stood far apart on spend and purchase count, whereas the remaining three categories shared similar activity levels and differed mostly in recency.

Because the features separated buyers so clearly, segment names are written back to the customer dimension in the star schema for the Power BI dashboard.

Marketing teams can now use a persona slicer in the Power BI report to isolate the 400 VIP Champions for targeted retention campaigns.

When segmenting customer data for business intelligence, do you write cluster labels directly into dimension tables or generate them dynamically?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center
text:
Evaluating credit risk works best when high precision comes before catching every single defaulted loan.

FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center is a personal portfolio project on credit risk and fraud detection. I built it because my father took a big loss in the market when a scam that had been going on was exposed; he was collateral damage, along with many other ordinary people.

Before deploying a classifier, I needed to determine whether Random Forest or XGBoost should decline risky loan applications. Rejecting qualified applicants creates friction, so scoring every application at 0.80 or more likely to default required a clear comparison between models.

So I trained both models on the same features and scored them on a held-out 20% of the synthetic loans, logging both runs in MLflow. Random Forest reached a ROC AUC of 0.9216 compared to 0.9179 for XGBoost, while delivering 0.9341 decline precision against 0.9132. XGBoost caught more default cases with a decline recall of 0.4456 versus 0.3427, but turned away 0.1143 of all applications while Random Forest declined 0.0859.

The answer made the choice clear. Random Forest went to production because it had the higher ROC AUC and the greater precision when declining an application.

When you tune probability thresholds for risk models, do you prioritize precision to protect valid applicants or recall to catch defaults?

#MachineLearning #DataEngineering
